content: Respiratory viruses are the primary cause of lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) and hospitalizations in infants and young children. Among these viruses, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the most significant infectious agent in this population. Palivizumab, an antibody administered intramuscularly once a month for five months during the first RSV season, is used to prevent severe RSV-related LRTIs in children. Due to its high cost, it is critical to evaluate whether palivizumab remains effective in preventing severe RSV disease in children. The objective of this study was to assess the effects of palivizumab in preventing severe RSV infections in children. To achieve this, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, up to October 2021. They also reviewed references, performed citation searches, and contacted study authors to identify additional studies. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), including cluster-RCTs, were included if they compared palivizumab (15 mg/kg monthly, up to five doses) with placebo, no intervention, or standard care in children aged 0 to 24 months, regardless of RSV infection history. The study selection, risk of bias assessment, and data extraction were performed using standard Cochrane methods. The primary outcomes evaluated were hospitalizations due to RSV infection, all-cause mortality, and adverse events. Secondary outcomes included hospitalizations due to respiratory-related illnesses, length of hospital stay, RSV infections, number of wheezing days, days requiring supplemental oxygen, intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay, and days requiring mechanical ventilation. Five studies involving a total of 3,343 participants were included in the analysis. All studies were parallel RCTs that assessed the effects of palivizumab (15 mg/kg monthly for up to five months) compared to placebo or no intervention in outpatient settings. One study also included hospitalized infants. Most of the studies focused on children at high risk of RSV infection due to comorbidities such as bronchopulmonary dysplasia and congenital heart disease. The risk of bias across all studies was generally low. The findings demonstrated that palivizumab significantly reduces hospitalizations due to RSV infection at two years of follow-up. The risk ratio (RR) was 0.44 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.30 to 0.64), with high-certainty evidence. In the placebo group, there were 98 hospitalizations per 1,000 participants, compared to 43 hospitalizations (range: 29 to 62) per 1,000 participants in the palivizumab group. Palivizumab likely has little to no effect on all-cause mortality at two years of follow-up. The RR for mortality was 0.69 (95% CI 0.42 to 1.15), with moderate-certainty evidence. In the placebo group, there were 23 deaths per 1,000 participants, compared to 16 deaths (range: 10 to 27) per 1,000 participants in the palivizumab group. Palivizumab likely results in little to no difference in adverse events at 150 days of follow-up. The RR for adverse events was 1.09 (95% CI 0.85 to 1.39), with moderate-certainty evidence. In the placebo group, there were 84 adverse events per 1,000 participants, compared to 91 adverse events (range: 71 to 117) per 1,000 participants in the palivizumab group. Palivizumab likely results in a slight reduction in hospitalizations due to respiratory-related illnesses at two years of follow-up. The RR was 0.78 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.97), with moderate-certainty evidence. Palivizumab may result in a substantial reduction in RSV infections at two years of follow-up. The RR was 0.33 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.55), with low-certainty evidence. In the placebo group, there were 195 cases of RSV infection per 1,000 participants, compared to 64 cases (range: 39 to 107) per 1,000 participants in the palivizumab group. Palivizumab also reduces the number of wheezing days at one year of follow-up. The RR was 0.39 (95% CI 0.35 to 0.44), with high-certainty evidence. In conclusion, the evidence suggests that palivizumab prophylaxis reduces hospitalizations due to RSV infection and has little to no effect on mortality or adverse events. Additionally, palivizumab results in a slight reduction in hospitalizations due to respiratory-related illnesses and may lead to a significant reduction in RSV infections. It also reduces the number of wheezing days. These findings are particularly relevant for children at high risk of RSV infection due to comorbidities. Further research is needed to evaluate the effects of palivizumab in children with other risk factors for severe RSV disease, such as immune deficiencies, and in populations with social determinants of health, including those in lowand middle-income countries, tropical regions, or living in poverty or overcrowded conditions.
